gtrig#1.en: Trigonometry: where the ratios come from

gtrig#2.en:
trigonometry → three · trigonometry → angled · trigonometry → measurement — the study of angles and of the angular relationships of triangles.

SOHCAHTOA only works in a right triangle. Opposite = across from θ. Adjacent = next to θ. Hypotenuse = across from the right angle.

sin θ = O/H = y/r  ·  cos θ = A/H = x/r  ·  tan θ = O/A = y/x

Picture a point moving round a circle: the radius stays the same, but θ, the x-coordinate and the y-coordinate all change. A ratio on its own means nothing — it only means something once you know its θ.

"The sine is 0,6" tells you nothing alone. Fix r, move the point, watch x and y — the ratio IS the angle.

gtrig#3.en: The Cartesian plane: All Strippers Take Cash

gtrig#4.en:
Going anticlockwise from quadrant ①: All positive · Strippers (sin only) · Take (tan only) · Cash (cos only).

①②③④
sin θ++−−
cos θ+−−+
tan θ+−+−

Why: cos θ = x/r and sin θ = y/r, and r is always positive (it's the radius) — so the sign is decided by x or y alone, never by r.

Quadrant ②: x is negative, y is positive, r is always positive → sin θ = y/r is +, cos θ = x/r is −.

gtrig#5.en: Special angles: the two triangles + Oats Are Healthy

gtrig#6.en:
Cut a square corner to corner → the 45-45-90 triangle (sides 1, 1, √2). Cut an equilateral triangle straight down the middle → the 30-60-90 triangle (sides 1, √3, 2).

Oats Are Healthy — the table, built in order: O · A · H down the side, 30° · 45° · 60° across the top:

30°45°60°
O11√3
A√311
H2√22

Values stay unrationalised (tan 30° = 1/√3, not √3/3). Quadrantal angles (0°, 90°, 180°, 270°) are read straight off the graph or the calculator, never memorised.

Masked identities: from sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 → sin²θ = 1 − cos²θ and cos²θ = 1 − sin²θ. Reciprocals — "look at the 3rd letter": cosec → sin, sec → cos, cot → tan.

tan 30° = O/A = 1/√3. sin 60° = √3/2. cos 90° = 0 (read off the graph).

gtrig#7.en: Co-functions: converting between sin and cos

gtrig#8.en:
Draw a right triangle's two acute angles two ways: θ at one corner, 90° − θ at the other. They share the SAME sides — just different names for opposite/adjacent — so:

sin θ = cos(90° − θ)  ·  cos θ = sin(90° − θ)

90° − θ is quadrant A — everything positive. 90° + θ has crossed into quadrant S — only sine stays positive. That's the trap:

cos(90° + θ) = −sin θ

Cosine is not sine, so cos(90° + θ) is negative. (Contrast: sin(90° + θ) = +cos θ — sine is fine there.)

Negative co-functions (further from the origin, same idea):

sin(θ − 90°) = −cos θ  ·  cos(θ − 90°) = sin θ
sin 40° = cos 50°. cos 120° = cos(90° + 30°) = −sin 30°.

gtrig#9.en: Reductions: rewriting angles as acute angles

gtrig#10.en:
Reductions = rewriting any angle as ± an acute angle. Every angle repeats every 360°, and every reduced ratio has the same size as the acute one it came from — the sign is the only thing that can change.

Three steps, in order:

① quadrant  →  ② reduction formula  →  ③ sign (All Strippers Take Cash)
positivenegative
S ②180° − θ−180° − θ
T ③180° + θθ − 180°
C ④360° − θ−θ  /  −360° − θ
A ①θ  /  360° + θθ − 360°

An angle in (−90°, 0°) is a C-angle straight off the wheel — form −θ, no rotation. Anything past a full turn (past 360°, or below −90°) gets ONE extra first step: add or take off 360°.

A reduction never swaps the ratio (sin stays sin) — only a co-function does that.

sin 210° = sin(180° + 30°) = −sin 30°. sin 510° = [−360°] sin 150° = sin(180° − 30°) = sin 30°.

gtrig#12.en:
Five checks to run before you commit to an answer:

  1. ① positive angle over 360°? → minus 360°. sin 520° = sin 160°
  2. ② negative angle under −90°? → add 360°. sin(−120°) = sin 240° (but an angle above −90° needs NO rotation at all)
  3. ③ squaring a reduced function? → reduce INSIDE block brackets first, then square: the minus dies. sin²210° = [−sin 30°]² = sin²30°, positive
  4. ④ the co-functions trap: cos(90° + θ) = −sin θ
  5. ⑤ co-functions with negative angles: sin(θ − 90°) = −cos θ  ·  cos(θ − 90°) = sin θ

Positive angles turn anti-clockwise; negative angles turn clockwise; co-functions convert between sin and cos.

"but why?" for Chip ⑤: let K = 90° − θ, so θ − 90° = −K, which sits in quadrant IV — where cos survives and sin flips.

gtrig#14.en:
Same machine as a numerical reduction — quadrant, formula, sign — but the value is left as the letter (x, θ, α…) instead of a number, so there's nothing to calculate.

Reduce every factor in place, keep the minus signs visible in brackets, then cancel:

cos(180° + θ)  =  −cos θ   ·   tan(θ − 180°)  =  +tan θ

A plain reduction NEVER swaps the ratio — sin stays sin, cos stays cos, tan stays tan. Only the three co-function forms (90° − θ, 90° + θ, θ − 90°) convert between sin and cos.

tan(180° + θ) · sin(360° − θ) / tan(360° − θ) = tan θ · (−sin θ) / (−tan θ) = sin θ.

gtrig#16.en:
You are given ONE ratio and ONE interval, and asked to work out the value of some expression. Five steps, in this order:

① isolate the function  ·  ② determine the quadrant  ·  ③ sketch the diagram  ·  ④ calculate the unknown side  ·  ⑤ substitute

Step ② is where the marks are. Two things were given, so you tick TWICE on one cross, in two different colours:

  • one colour for the quadrants the ratio's sign allows (All Strippers Take Cash)
  • a second colour for the quadrants the interval allows

The quadrant with two ticks is the one you sketch in. That overlap is the whole idea.

Then Pythagoras for the missing side — and two habits that make it read as yours:

y² = 13² − (−12)²   (pyth)
y = ±5  →  ∴ y = 5

The given negative stays inside the square, and the ± line is followed by a ∴ line that picks the sign off the quadrant. r is always positive bc it is the radius — it never takes the minus.

3 tan θ − 4 = 0 with θ ∈ (180°; 360°). tan is + in ① and ③; the interval gives ③ and ④ → ③. Sketch x = −3, y = −4, r = 5. Then 25 sin²θ − 5 cos θ = 25(−4/5)² − 5(−3/5) = 16 + 3 = 19.

gtrig#18.en:
When in doubt, go LEFT. You work the left-hand side, top to bottom, until it turns into the right-hand side — and you close with = RHS. Never squeeze both sides towards the middle.

There are only four moves, and every question is one of them:

  • fractions → find the LCD (every different bottom, multiplied together)
  • a bracket squared / two brackets → multiply out (products)
  • a common factor → take it out
  • a division by a fraction → flip it and multiply

And two things you keep in your pocket:

tan θ = sin θ/cos θ   ·   sin²θ + cos²θ = 1

The masked identities are that second one rearranged: sin²θ = 1 − cos²θ and cos²θ = 1 − sin²θ. A 1 with nothing under it gets a denominator of 1 before it can join a fraction.

1/cos²θ − 1 = 1/cos²θ − 1/1 = (1 − cos²θ)/cos²θ = sin²θ/cos²θ = tan²θ.

gtrig#19.en: Super special sums: the flamingo & the short-cut

gtrig#20.en:
You are told something like cos 20° = t and asked for everything else in terms of t. A bare value cannot be read off a triangle — so stand it on a 1. That is the flamingo:

cos 20° = t = t/1 = a/h

Now t is the adjacent side, 1 is the hypotenuse, and the triangle draws itself in the first quadrant. Pythagoras finds the third side, and then you just read the answers off the picture.

The Short-cut — three ready-made triangles:

givenadjacentoppositehypotenuse
tan θ = t1t√(t² + 1)
sin θ = t√(1 − t²)t1
cos θ = 1/t1√(t² − 1)t

√(1 − t²) or √(t² − 1)? Pythagoras decides: the HYPOTENUSE squared is the one that gets the plus, so the missing leg is (hypotenuse)² − (other leg)². If the 1 is the hypotenuse you get √(1 − t²); if the letter is the hypotenuse you get √(t² − 1).

If the question asks about a different angle, reduce it to the acute one first, then read it off.

cos 20° = t. Then sin 20° = √(1 − t²), tan 20° = √(1 − t²)/t, and cos 160° = −cos 20° = −t.

gtrig#22.en:
Before you solve anything, name the type. There are six, and they are always in this order:

  • ① function alone — one ratio, one number. Isolate it, then ref ∠ and quadrants. (don't type − into the calculator)
  • ② same angles — sin and cos with the SAME angle. Divide every term by cos and it becomes one tan. also: divide by cos (tan θ)
  • ③ common factor — take the factor out, then each bracket separately = 0. take 0 as +
  • ④ grouping — four terms. Group them in pairs; the brackets left over must come out the same.
  • ⑤ trinomial — three terms, one function squared and one not. K-method; if the middle term is a different function, a masked identity first. also: trinomial with a masked identity
  • ⑥ co-functions — sin and cos with DIFFERENT angles. Make both sides the same function, then match the brackets. no ref. ∠ · also: make both cos

If a factor asks a sine or cosine for something outside [−1 ; 1], write ∴ no solution — not "undefined", not "no real solution".

2 sin²x + 5 sin x − 3 = 0 is ⑤. Let K = sin x → 2K² + 5K − 3 = 0 → (2K − 1)(K + 3) = 0 → sin x = 1/2, or sin x = −3 which has no solution.

gtrig#23.en: General solution: the last two decisions

gtrig#24.en:
Once the ratio is on its own, everything comes down to two things: which quadrants, and what the reference angle is.

The cross. A vertical line and a horizontal line, with a ✓ in each quadrant you are using — top-right is I, top-left is II, bottom-left is III, bottom-right is IV. The sign of the value picks the pair (All Strippers Take Cash).

The reference angle comes from the POSITIVE value. Don't type − into the calculator. The minus already did its job when it chose the quadrants; only the size of the number is left.

cos θ = −2/5  →  ✓ in II and III  ·  ref. ∠ = 66,42°

tan gets ONE line. tan repeats every 180°, so the second quadrant line adds nothing — a waste of time.

Boundary values follow the same sign rule — All Strippers Take Cash: cos θ = 1 → cos is positive → tick I and IV, ref ∠ = 0 · sin θ = −1 → sin is negative → tick III and IV, ref ∠ = 90° · cos θ = −1 → tick II and III, ref ∠ = 0 · sin θ = 0 → ref ∠ = 0, tick I and II.

Co-functions have NO reference angle at all. Two different angles means there is nothing to take an inverse of — you make both sides the same function and match the brackets instead.

sin x = 1/2 → ✓ in I and II, ref ∠ = 30°. But sin(x + 80°) = sin 2x → no reference angle.

gtrig#26.en:
Undefined ↳ denominator = 0. A fraction breaks when its bottom is nothing at all, so the question is only ever "what is on the bottom?"

The routine:

  1. list every denominator — on both sides of the equation
  2. set each one = 0
  3. solve each one as an ordinary general solution
  4. read the interval off the list

Two things people get wrong. Numerators do not count — a top of zero is a perfectly ordinary answer. And tan does not get its own line: tan x is sin x over cos x, so its cos x is already on your list.

tan x + cos x/(1 + sin x) = 1/cos x → the denominators are 1 + sin x and cos x. So 1 + sin x = 0 (sin x = −1, ref ∠ = 90°, III and IV) or cos x = 0 (ref ∠ = 90°, I and IV). On (−180°; 180°) that gives x ∈ {−90°; 90°}.
